Longjaw thryssa (Thryssa setirostris) is a coastal clupeiform species that attains a maximum recorded total length of 18 centimeters [Li = 18 centimeters], a relatively modest size among the Engraulidae. Substantial variation in growth trajectories has been observed across its range, which extends from the western Indian Ocean through the Indonesian Archipelago. Field surveys of this zooplanktivorous fish indicate that total length at sexual maturation, defined by the onset of gonadal development, occurs at approximately 15 centimeters [Lp = approximately 15 centimeters]. This length threshold marks a significant physiological transition, after which individuals begin to allocate increasing somatic resources toward reproductive tissues. The species is known to inhabit estuarine and inshore waters where turbid conditions and high prey densities prevail, likely supporting the relatively rapid somatic growth required to reach these size benchmarks within a single annual cycle.

Reproductive investment in Longjaw thryssa has been quantified under controlled conditions maintained at 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], a temperature representative of its tropical coastal habitats. Under these thermal conditions, females produce an estimated clutch size of 45 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 45 eggs per spawning event] and exhibit a spawning frequency of one event each day [F_R_i = one event each day]. This high frequency of gamete release is characteristic of engraulid species that employ a batch-spawning strategy, allowing the population to spread reproductive effort across an extended breeding season. The volumetric constraints of the body cavity likely limit maximum clutch volume, while the energetic demands of daily oocyte maturation require a continuous and abundant supply of planktonic prey. Temperature-mediated metabolic rates are thought to underpin this rapid reproductive cycling, as evidenced by lower spawning frequencies observed in cooler, higher-latitude populations of congeneric species.

The larval and early juvenile stages of Longjaw thryssa are brief, reflecting the selective pressures of predation risk in plankton-rich, nearshore environments. The embryonic development period, from egg fertilisation to chorion rupture and emergence of the yolk-sac larva, spans approximately three days [ab = approximately three days] when incubation occurs at 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C]. Upon eclosion, the prolarva carries a substantial yolk reserve that supports endotrophic development during the critical period before mouth opening and first exogenous feeding. The wet weight recorded for these newly emerged larvae is just 0.00027 grams [Wwb = 0.00027 grams], an extraordinarily small initial mass that underscores the high fecundity required to offset extreme larval mortality. This birth weight is consistent with an egg diameter of approximately 0.8 millimeters, which is typical of pelagic-spawning engraulids that produce small, buoyant oocytes.

Somatic growth following the larval period proceeds rapidly, with juveniles transitioning through the postflexion stage before metamorphosis into demersal, post-settlement fingerlings. The ultimate wet weight achieved by adults of Thryssa setirostris, based on a representative specimen series collected from trawl surveys, is 66.67 grams [Wwi = 66.67 grams]. This asymptotic mass is attained once the fish reach their maximum total length of 18 centimeters and appears to be constrained by the gape-limited feeding morphology of the species, a value comparable to that of other small-bodied engraulids. In comparison, the wet weight at the onset of sexual maturity, corresponding to a total length of 15 centimeters, has been estimated at 37.5 grams [Wwp = 37.5 grams]. The ratio of maturation mass to ultimate mass, approximately 0.56, indicates a moderate degree of deferred reproduction, whereby individuals channel substantial energy into continued somatic expansion even after puberty onset.

Longevity records for Longjaw thryssa under the thermal regime typical of its tropical distribution, approximately 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], indicate a maximum lifespan of 350 days [am = 350 days]. This short life expectancy, less than a full year, classifies the species as an annual or near-annual teleost, a common life-history strategy among small, fast-maturing marine clupeiforms adapted to highly seasonal productivity pulses. The brief maximum lifespan, combined with the high daily reproductive rate and early maturation, places Thryssa setirostris firmly within an opportunistic or periodic life-history continuum. Post-reproductive senescence is rapid, with individuals typically showing signs of physiological deterioration shortly after the cessation of spawning activity. Such a compressed life cycle is viable only in environments where prey resources are predictably abundant, allowing the population to replace itself completely within each annual cohort before the onset of age-related mortality.
